The Scientific Method and Lab Safety: Science answers questions about nature by testing ideas against evidence. The scientific method is a flexible path: ask a question, research, form a testable hypothesis, run a controlled experiment, analyze the data, draw a conclusion and share the results. A controlled experiment changes only the independent variable, measures the dependent variable and keeps every other variable the same. A control group is used for comparison. A theory is a well-tested explanation, not a guess. Data support or fail to support a hypothesis; they never prove it for every case. In the lab wear goggles, follow directions, never taste chemicals and report spills and accidents at once.
SI Units and Measurement: Scientists use the International System of Units (SI). The base units are the meter for length, the kilogram for mass, the second for time and the kelvin for temperature. Prefixes change the size of a unit: kilo means 1000, centi 1/100, milli 1/1000, micro one millionth and mega one million. Derived units combine base units, such as m/s for speed, m^2 for area and kg/m^3 for density. Liquid volume is often in liters, where 1 L = 1000 mL. Kelvin equals Celsius plus 273 (273.15 exactly). Accuracy is closeness to the true value and precision is how closely repeated measurements agree. Read instruments at eye level and estimate one digit beyond the smallest mark.
Scientific Notation and Significant Figu: Scientific notation writes a number as a times 10^n with 1 <= a < 10. Moving the decimal to the left gives a positive exponent and moving it to the right gives a negative exponent. Significant figures show how precise a measurement is. Nonzero digits are always significant, zeros between nonzero digits are significant, leading zeros are not, and trailing zeros count only when there is a decimal point. When multiplying or dividing keep as many significant figures as the least precise number. When adding or subtracting keep as many decimal places as the least precise number. Exact counted numbers have unlimited significant figures.
Unit Conversions: Dimensional analysis converts units by multiplying by conversion factors that equal one, written so the unwanted unit cancels. Useful factors are 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 h = 60 min = 3600 s and 1 in = 2.54 cm. To change km/h to m/s multiply by 1000/3600, which is the same as dividing by 3.6. Always write the units with every number and check that only the wanted unit is left. A result that is far too big or too small is a sign that a factor was upside down.
Graphs and Data Analysis: Graphs show how two variables are related. The independent variable goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis. A good graph has a title, labeled axes with units and an even scale. Line graphs show change, bar graphs compare categories. A best-fit line follows the trend of the points. The slope of a line is rise over run and has units of y over x. A straight line through the origin means the variables are directly proportional. Reading between measured points is interpolation and reading beyond them is extrapolation.
